name: Scar tattooing / micropigmentation

card.summary: Cosmetic tattooing that deposits pigment in scars or pale skin to blend them with surrounding skin; documented clinically but with little outcome data.
card.aka: Medical tattooing, scar camouflage tattoo, dermal micropigmentation
card.note: Pigment is semi-permanent and matching skin tone is difficult; the Wikipedia overview gives no outcome data.

quick.overview:
Scar tattooing, or micropigmentation, places pigment into the skin to make scars, pale patches or missing structures such as an areola look more like the surrounding skin. It belongs to the broader field of medical tattooing.[1]

Sources reviewed describe uses and history but give no controlled outcome data, and the evidence base cited by Wikipedia consists mainly of patient satisfaction reviews and general reviews of medical tattooing.
quick.mechanism: A tattoo device deposits pigment in the dermis, in a realistic style meant to imitate normal skin color. For scars, people may alternatively choose a decorative design that covers the area.[1]
quick.risks: Wikipedia's article does not detail risks specific to scar camouflage. It notes that diabetes can impair wound healing, so timing and location of a medical tattoo may need care in people with diabetes.[1] General tattoo risks include infection and allergic reactions.

lead: Scar tattooing, also called micropigmentation, is a form of medical tattooing intended to hide a medical condition or the result of its treatment, typically in a realistic style.[1] It is used to camouflage scars, reduce the visibility of vitiligo patches, and recreate areolas after mastectomy or chest surgery.[1]

In looksmaxxing discussions it appears among "hardmaxxing" procedures for scars. Published information reviewed here describes its history and uses but offers little outcome data; Wikipedia cites a 2021 systematic review of patient satisfaction and older reviews of medical tattooing without summarising their findings.[1]

paras: Medical tattoos are cosmetic tattoos meant to hide a condition or the results of its treatment, usually in a realistic style. For scars, people may alternatively choose a decorative cover-up design.[1]

Documented uses include covering scars and simulating fingernails, reducing the visibility of vitiligo patches, and replacing a removed areola or filling pigment loss after free nipple grafts following mastectomy, reconstruction, breast reduction or chest masculinization.[1] Related microblading is used to restore eyebrows lost to alopecia or trichotillomania.[1]
Wikipedia reports that in 1835 the German doctor Pauli tattooed skin lesions including nevi with mercury sulfide and white lead, and that lip scars were tattooed with cinnabar starting in 1911.[1]
The overview describes no risks specific to scar camouflage other than noting that diabetes can impair wound healing and may affect the choice of location and timing.[1]

No studies found of scar tattooing as such in the trial registry material reviewed. Wikipedia cites a 2021 systematic review of patient satisfaction with medical tattooing and earlier reviews without reporting their results.[1] A separate registered trial (NCT04046679) examines a bleomycin infusion technique to repigment achromic scars; it is a different method from tattooing.[2]

timeline.event: Pauli tattoos skin lesions including nevi with mercury sulfide and white lead.[1]
Lip scars begin to be tattooed with cinnabar.[1]
